title: Guru Amar Das's gurpurab
hookLine: remembered at Goindval, the well of eighty-four steps
last: A HYMN FOR EVERY TURN · THE MONTH BEGINS · FULL MOON · DATES · THE POOL · THE SCRIPT AND THE KITCHEN.

lines: A SONG AT THE BUTTER CHURN.
cards: Here's a life that runs the other way from the usual story. Tradition remembers a man who spent most of his life as a devout pilgrim of his own tradition, walking to the Ganges again and again.

Then, already old, he hears a young woman singing Guru Nanak's hymns while she churns butter, and everything changes. Years later, past seventy, tradition says, he becomes the third Guru. Today: baoli.

teach.h: A PILGRIM, AND A SONG AT THE CHURN.
teach.b: The young woman at the churn was Bibi Amro, Guru Angad's daughter, married into his family.
Tradition says he was so moved that he went to Khadur, and for years served Guru Angad, carrying water from the river before dawn, every day.
He became Guru, tradition says, past seventy, and settled at Goindval, on the river Beas. Two things there are remembered on his gurpurab. The first is the langar.
Tradition says he asked everyone who came to eat in the free kitchen first, sitting together on the floor, before meeting him: high caste and low, rich and poor, side by side.
Sikhs remember a saying linked to him: first the pangat, the row of people eating, then the sangat, the gathering.
The second is the baoli, a stepwell. He had a deep well built at Goindval, with steps leading down to the water: eighty-four of them. Water open to everyone, with no caste rule at the bottom.
Today some pilgrims walk down to the water reciting the Japji Sahib once on each step, a long, slow devotion.

Some Sikhs connect the eighty-four steps to the old Indian idea of eighty-four lakh lives; others keep it simply as a practice of patience, and some point out that Gurbani speaks of liberation by grace and the Name, not by counting.
Either way, it's a picture of the third Guru himself: going down, step by step, slowly, toward water.

how: On Guru Amar Das's gurpurab, gurdwaras hold kirtan and langar, and at Goindval Sahib some pilgrims descend the baoli, reciting Japji Sahib on each of its eighty-four steps.

games.q: you've come to Goindval to meet the third Guru. what does tradition say comes first?
o: eating in the langar, side by side with everyone.
a test of your scripture knowledge.
games.why: first the pangat, then the sangat: everyone ate together on the floor before meeting the Guru.

practice: Pour a glass of water and sit with it, thinking of the people at Goindval walking down eighty-four steps to reach it. Then drink in small, slow sips, noticing the cool of it, and breathe between sips.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each sip.

wordCard.voice: Baoli, the stepwell of eighty-four steps Guru Amar Das built at Goindval, remembered along with the langar where all sat together.

orig.note: Punjabi: a stepwell; the baoli at Goindval has eighty-four steps.

carryVoice: Your line: eighty-four steps. No step skipped, and not one of them rushed. Day six hundred eighty-six, done.
